newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: I&J year profit seen bouncing off low base.
newsitem.headline: I&J year profit seen bouncing off low base.

text.p: South African foods group Irvin & Johnson Ltd is set to post a big rise in year profit next week, but analysts warned on Friday the firm is bouncing off a low base.
Last year the firm recorded a steep profits drop after being hit by losses at its Namibian joint-venture Kuiseb Fish Products and a loss on the sale of an Australian wholesale business.
This year analysts are predicting a largely better fish harvest in South African and Namibian waters and the firm should meet a forecast of healthy growth that it made in February.
"They are coming off a very low base. Fishing in South African waters has been pretty mixed, but it has been a bit better in Namibian deep sea fishing," said one analyst.

Analysts saw the firm posting earnings per share on a range of 31.0 to 32.6 cents, against 18.0 cents last time. The dividend is seen rising to a range of 11.0 cents to 13.4, up from 10 cents last time.
The consensus figures were for earnings of 31.9 cents and a shareholder payout of 12.5 cents.

The firm has recently taken steps to improve its Namibian operations by establishing a new joint-venture firm made up of Kuiseb and Consortium Fisheries. The new firm has been called Hangana Seafood and is 40 percent owned by Kuiseb.
The move has been welcomed, but comes too late to affect the firm's operations this year. "It is a good move to get maximum benefit out of a still difficult market," said another analyst.

However, one thing that could hit the firm this year is the poor performance of Rainbow Chicken Ltd. I&J has a distributor agreement with Rainbow and the firm's lacklustre showing recently could bite into profit at I&J's distribution arm.
Last month the poultry broiler producer said it will report losses significantly higher than expected in the half-year to September in the latest of a string of profit warnings and poor results.
"Rainbow has had another terrible year," said John Moses, analyst at Societe Generale Frankel Pollack.
